solutions.latex: \exfigure{33_q11_1}

Tank $B$: $V=30(t-15)$ for $t\ge15$. This line starts at $(15,0)$ and rises $30$ litres each minute; drawn on the grid in part (a), it meets the Tank $A$ line at $t=29$.

\exfigure{33_q11_1}

Check algebraically:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000-20t &= 30(t-15)\\ 1000-20t &= 30t-450\\ 1450 &= 50t\\ t &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The tanks hold the same volume after $29$ minutes.
criteria: Draws the graph of volume for tank $B$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $t\ge15$, the total volume is
$$\begin{aligned} (1000-20t)+30(t-15) &= 1000\\ 10t-450 &= 0\\ t &= 45 \end{aligned}$$
(For $0<t<15$ the total is $1000-20t<1000$.) Tank $A$ is not yet empty at $t=45$ ($V=100$), so the model still applies.

$\therefore$ $t=45$ minutes.

parts.latex:
Katrina runs a business refurbishing old computers.

The cost, $C$ dollars, of refurbishing $n$ computers is given by $C=3n^2+100$.

The income, $I$ dollars, received from selling $n$ computers is given by $I=80n$.

Determine the minimum and maximum number of computers that Katrina can refurbish and sell to make a profit.

solutions.latex:
Solve $3n^2+100=80n$.

$$\begin{aligned}3n^2-80n+100&=0\\ n&=\dfrac{80\pm\sqrt{(-80)^2-4\times 3\times 100}}{2\times 3}\\ n&=1.315,\ 25.352\end{aligned}$$

Katrina will make a profit when $I>C$ and this occurs for $2\le n\le 25$, where $n$ represents the number of computers refurbished and sold.

Hence, the minimum number is 2 and the maximum number is 25 in order to make a profit.
criteria: Solves quadratic equation and finds two non-integer solutions for $n$
Forms quadratic equation to find break-even points, or equivalent merit

An object is thrown vertically upwards from the top of a tall building. The height, $h$ metres, of the object above the ground after $t$ seconds is given by

$$h=45+12t-2t^2.$$

What is the vertical distance, in metres, that the object rises above the top of the building?

solutions.latex:
The top of the building is the height at $t=0$:
$$h(0)=45$$
The maximum height occurs at $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} h(3)&=45+12(3)-2(3)^2\\ &=63 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the object rises $63-45=18$ m above the top of the building.

638.stem: Eric is organising a gala dinner. The function centre will charge him \$2 000 to hire the room and he needs to pay a catering company \$80 per person for food.

figures.cap: income and cost lines C against n

parts.latex: Write an equation for the cost \$$C$ of hosting the event for $n$ people.
What is the profit if 75 people attend the dinner?

solutions.latex:
The cost is $\$2000$ for the room plus $\$80$ for each of the $n$ people:
$$C=80n+2000$$

From the graph, the income and cost lines intersect at $n=50$ (and $C=\$6000$).

$\therefore$ 50 people are required to break even.

From the graph, when 75 people attend, the income is $\$9000$ and the costs are $\$8000$:
$$9000-8000=1000$$
$\therefore$ The profit is $\$1000$ when 75 people attend.

1329.stem: 25 students sit an exam with a total mark out of 40. For each of the 25 students, the number $x$ of the lessons missed and the number $y$ of the marks lost on the test were recorded. The total number of marks lost was 230 more than the total number of lessons missed. The correlation coefficient between lessons missed and marks lost was $r=0.81$ and the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed has equation $y=1.5x+6$.

parts.latex: Describe the nature and strength of the correlation between lessons missed and marks lost.
parts.note: Describing correlation: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06 / MST-12-S2-08

parts.latex: Given that the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, find the mean number of lessons missed and marks lost.
Find the equation of the least squares regression line of marks gained on lessons missed.
parts.note: Regression line of a transformed response: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06 / MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex: Strong, positive, linear relationship

$y=1.5x+6$

Total marks lost $=25\bar{y}$

Total lessons missed $=25\bar{x}$

The total marks lost is 230 more than the total lessons missed:
$$25\bar{x}+230=25\bar{y}\quad(1)$$
The line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$:
$$\bar{y}=1.5\bar{x}+6\quad(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}25\bar{x}+230&=25(1.5\bar{x}+6)\\ 25\bar{x}+230&=37.5\bar{x}+150\\ 80&=12.5\bar{x}\\ \bar{x}&=6.4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{y}&=1.5(6.4)+6\\ &=15.6\end{aligned}$$

Since the test is out of 40, marks gained $=40-y$.

$\therefore$ least squares regression line for marks gained on lessons missed:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Marks gained}&=40-(1.5x+6)\\ &=40-6-1.5x\\ &=-1.5x+34\end{aligned}$$

1649.stem: The population of a town in NSW has shown a linear decline in the years 2011 to 2019. In 2011 the population was 34300 people. In 2019 it was 27740 people.

parts.latex: Write a linear equation expressing the population of the town, $P$, as a function of $t$, the number of years since 2011.
If the town is still experiencing a linear decline, what will the population be in 2025?

solutions.latex:
The population is linear, so $P=34300+kt$.

In 2019, $t=8$ and $P=27740$:
$$\begin{aligned} 27740&=34300+8k \\ k&=-820 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore P=-820t+34300$$
criteria: Correct working finding the declining rate, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In 2025, $t=14$:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=-820\times14+34300 \\ &=22\,820 \text{ people} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The formula for the cost involved in selling $N$ Midiens in a day is $C=10N+300$. What is the cost when 20 Midiens are sold in a day?
Draw the line representing the equation $C=10N+300$ on the graph on page 12.
How many Midiens would they need to sell in a day to break even?
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

parts.latex: How much profit or loss would they make on a day where they sold 30 Midiens? Clearly state profit or loss.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $N=20$ into $C=10N+300$:
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 10\times 20+300 \\ &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the cost is } \$500$$

The line $C=10N+300$ has $C$-intercept $300$ (fixed costs), and from part (a) passes through $(20,\,500)$. A second point is $N=40$, $C=700$.

\exfigure{394_q14_s1}
criteria: Plots one correct point, or draws a line with the correct gradient, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Break-even occurs where income equals cost, $I=C$.
$$\begin{aligned} 30N &= 10N+300 \\ 20N &= 300 \\ N &= 15 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{they must sell 15 Midiens}$$

When $N=30$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{income} &= 30\times 30 = \$900 \\ \text{cost} &= 10\times 30+300 = \$600 \\ \text{profit} &= 900-600 = \$300 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{a profit of } \$300$$

1974.stem: Jamie owns a company producing and selling pizzas. The income function of $y=20x$ is shown on the graph below, where $x$ is the number of pizzas sold. The cost of producing these pizzas includes a set up cost of \$50 and additional costs of \$2 per pizza.

figures.cap: grid with income line y=20x from the origin, y axis to 150 and x axis to 14
solution sketch: cost line y=2x+50 drawn on the grid with the income line

parts.latex: Write the cost function in the form $y=mx+c$

Sketch the cost function on the axis below:

\exfigure{416_q13_1}
Hence, determine Jamie's break even point.
can_use: Simultaneous equations
Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

solutions.latex:
The cost is the set-up cost plus $\$2$ for each of the $x$ pizzas:
$$y=2x+50$$

\exfigure{416_q13_s1}

The cost function $y=2x+50$ is a straight line with $y$-intercept $50$ and gradient $2$.
criteria: Draws a straight line with the correct $y$-intercept or gradient, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Break even is where income equals cost:
$$\begin{aligned}20x&=2x+50\\ 18x&=50\\ x&=\dfrac{25}{9}\approx2.78\end{aligned}$$
At this point $y=20\cdot\dfrac{25}{9}=\dfrac{500}{9}\approx55.56$. Pizzas are sold whole: for $2$ pizzas the income is $\$40$ and the cost $\$54$, and for $3$ pizzas the income is $\$60$ and the cost $\$56$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Jamie must sell }3\text{ pizzas to break even}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y&=16-2\times 4 \\ &=8 \end{aligned}$$
The dimensions are $4$ m by $8$ m.

parts.latex:
A basketball player shoots a ball from a height of 2 metres into a hoop 14 metres away. The hoop 3 metres from the ground. After moving 5 metres horizontally, the ball reaches a height of 4 metres from the ground. This information is shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1612_q20_1}

The path of the ball can be modelled by the quadratic function

$$y = ax^2 + bx + c,$$

where $y$ represents the height of the ball from the ground, $x$ is the horizontal displacement from the basketball player, and $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$ that best model the path of the ball.

solutions.latex:
Place axes with the player at the origin.

\exfigure{1612_q20_s2}

The ball passes through $(0, 2)$, $(5, 4)$ and $(14, 3)$.

Substituting $(0, 2)$ gives $c = 2$, so $y = ax^2 + bx + 2$.

Substituting $(5, 4)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 25a + 5b + 2 \\ 2 &= 25a + 5b \\ a &= \dfrac{2 - 5b}{25} &&(1) \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $(14, 3)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 196a + 14b + 2 \\ 1 &= 196a + 14b &&(2) \end{aligned}$$

Substituting (1) into (2):

$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 196\left(\dfrac{2 - 5b}{25}\right) + 14b \\ 25 &= 196(2 - 5b) + 350b \\ 25 &= 392 - 980b + 350b \\ -367 &= -630b \\ b &= \dfrac{367}{630} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting into (1):

$$a = \dfrac{2 - 5\left(\frac{367}{630}\right)}{25} = -\dfrac{23}{630}$$

$$\therefore\ a = -\dfrac{23}{630},\ b = \dfrac{367}{630},\ c = 2$$
criteria: Finds the value of $c$ and develops simultaneous equations to solve for $a$ and $b$, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $c$, or equivalent merit

4274.stem:
Jamjet Industries produce galvanised bolts for the roofing industry. Due to manufacturing constraints, the maximum number of bolts they can produce in a month is 120 000.

The cost of production is \$50 000 plus 95 cents per bolt.

The bolts are sold for \$1.75 each and the graph that represents Jamjet's revenue, $R$, appears on the axes below.

\exfigure{1310_q12a_1}

figures.cap: graph of revenue R = 1.75n, cost axis up to 200000, n up to 120000

parts.latex: Find the linear equation for the cost, $C$, of producing $n$ bolts.
What is the practical significance of the gradient of the line in (a) ?
Find the number of bolts Jamjet must sell in a month to break even.
What is the maximum monthly profit attainable by Jamjet ?

solutions.latex:
The cost is a fixed \$50 000 plus \$0.95 per bolt.
$$C = 50000 + 0.95n$$
The gradient of the cost line is $0.95$, so it represents the cost of production per bolt (the rate at which cost increases for each extra bolt).
criteria: Correct answer; must reference rate in some way

solutions.latex:
Break-even occurs when revenue equals cost, $1.75n = C$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1.75n &= 50000 + 0.95n \\ 0.8n &= 50000 \\ n &= 62500 \end{aligned}$$
Jamjet must sell 62 500 bolts.

Profit is revenue minus cost.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 1.75n - (50000 + 0.95n) \\ &= 0.8n - 50000 \end{aligned}$$
Profit increases with $n$, so it is greatest at the maximum production $n = 120000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 0.8\times 120000 - 50000 \\ &= \$46000 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct profit expression, or substitutes $n = 120000$ into their expression for profit, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By developing and solving a pair of simultaneous equations, show that the number of spectators as a function of ticket price can be expressed as $N = -100P + 17500$.

The revenue generated from an event, $R$, is calculated using $R = N \times P$.

What is the maximum revenue generated from this event?
can_use: Solving optimisation problems

parts.latex:
The manager of this event wants the tennis arena to be filled with 15000 spectators.

Show that this will result in a revenue loss of \$390625.

solutions.latex:
Substitute the two known values into $N = mP + c$.

When $P=50$, $N=12500$:
$$12500 = 50m+c \qquad (1)$$
When $P=35$, $N=14000$:
$$14000 = 35m+c \qquad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 1500 &= -15m \\ m &= -100 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 12500 &= 50(-100)+c \\ c &= 17500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ N = -100P+17500$$
criteria: Correctly solves the equations simultaneously to obtain either $m$ or $c$, or equivalent merit
Correctly develops and attempts to solve the simultaneous equations

solutions.latex:
Revenue is
$$R = (-100P+17500)P = -100P^2+17500P$$
This is a concave-down quadratic, so the maximum is at the vertex:
$$P = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = \dfrac{-17500}{2(-100)} = 87.5$$
When $P=87.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} R &= -100(87.5)^2+17500(87.5) \\ &= \$765\,625 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum revenue} = \$765\,625$$
criteria: Correctly finds the quadratic equation that represents the revenue, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $N=15000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 15000 &= -100P+17500 \\ P &= 25 \end{aligned}$$
Revenue at this price:
$$\begin{aligned} R &= -100(25)^2+17500(25) \\ &= \$375\,000 \end{aligned}$$
Revenue loss:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{loss} &= 765\,625-375\,000 \\ &= \$390\,625 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the price when $N=15000$, or equivalent merit

The glider starts at the top of the tower, so the vertical ($h$) intercept is $c = 60$.

It loses $5$ metres each second, so the gradient is

$$m = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = -\dfrac{5}{1} = -5$$

Hence the equation is

$$h = -5t + 60$$
criteria: Draws the correct straight-line graph, or gives the correct equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The stone reaches the ground after $6$ seconds.

Substitute $t = 6$ into the glider equation.

$$\begin{aligned} h &= -5(6) + 60 \\ &= 30 \end{aligned}$$

After $6$ seconds the height of the glider is $30$ metres.

meta.format_note: Added the substitution line from the equation in (b); the source stated only the result.

5074.stem:
Michael has a small manufacturing business.

The cost of manufacturing is given by the equation $C=50x+200$ and the income earned is given by the equation $I=100x$, where $x$ is the number of items that the business has manufactured.

criteria: Graphs one correct line, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The business breaks even when $C=I$:
$$\begin{aligned}50x+200&=100x\\ 200&=50x\\ x&=4\end{aligned}$$
Break even at $4$ items.

5226.stem:
A mixture is to be made of two foods $A$ and $B$. The two foods $A$, $B$ contain nutrients $P$ and $Q$ as shown below:

\extable{1274_q15_t1}

The mixture contains 8 ounces of $P$ and 6 ounces of $Q$.

For example: one part of $A$ and 3 parts of $B$ will make 8 ounces of $P$ i.e.., $A+3B=8$

parts.latex: Use the similar method to form an equation for nutrient $Q$.
Solve the two equations simultaneously to find the values of $A$ and $B$.

solutions.latex:
Food $A$ has 2 parts of $Q$ and food $B$ has 1 part of $Q$ in the table, and the mixture has 6 ounces of $Q$.

$$2A+B=6$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} A+3B &= 8 &&(1) \\ 2A+B &= 6 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$

Multiply (1) by 2.

$$2A+6B=16$$

Subtract (2).

$$5B=10,\ \text{so } B=2$$

Substitute $B=2$ in (2).

$$2A+2=6,\ \text{so } A=2$$

$$\therefore\ A=2 \text{ and } B=2$$
criteria: Finds one variable correctly, or equivalent merit
Eliminates one variable, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Koolara High School wants to sell a new sports shirt to its students at \$40 each. To manufacture the shirts, the schools pays a fixed cost of \$595, as well as \$33 per shirt. By writing a pair of simultaneous equations, calculate how many shirts the school must sell in order to break-even.

solutions.latex:
Let $x$ be the number of shirts.

Cost: $C=595+33x$

Revenue: $R=40x$

Break-even occurs when $C=R$.
$$\begin{aligned} 595+33x&=40x\\ 7x&=595\\ x&=85 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the school must sell 85 shirts.
criteria: Correctly shows an equation for either cost or revenue, or equivalent merit

5610.stem:
The NSGHS brick company manufactures bricks for the building industry. The production capacity for the year is 100 000 standard bricks. The cost of production is fixed at $\$60\,000$ plus $\$0.60$ per brick. The selling price of each brick is $\$1.60$. The equation of the revenue ($R$) is shown on the graph below. The $y$-axis displays the cost/revenue in dollars and the $x$-axis represents the amount of bricks.

\exfigure{1289_q14_1}

figures.cap: graph of revenue R=1.6x
solution sketch: cost line C=60000+0.6x drawn in blue on the printed revenue graph

parts.latex: Find the equation for the cost ($C$) of $x$ bricks and plot this graph on the grid above.
How many bricks must be sold to break even?
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

criteria: Writes the equation or plots the graph, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Kept source's \exfigure.

solutions.latex:
Break even when cost equals revenue, $C=R$, where $R=1.6x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 60000+0.6x&=1.6x\\ x&=60000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 60\,000 \text{ bricks must be sold to break even.}$$
